name: Palula
confidence_why: Liljegren's 2016 reference grammar, backed by Liljegren and Haider's 2009 IPA illustration, describes a contrastive, lexically placed mora-based pitch accent with minimal pairs, and the only dissent is Morgenstierne's brief 1941 field notes, which describe quantity-driven stress and report noticing no tone but are hedged and rest on far less material than the later long-term fieldwork. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Liljegren 2016.

catalog_quote: "Main stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical root. One of the vocalic moras of the stressed syllable receives pitch accent, phonetically realised as: a) high level or high falling on a short vowel [ˊ] ... b) low rising on a long vowel [ˇ] ... or c) high falling on a long vowel [ˆ] ... Pitch accent is contrastive, as illustrated in (1)." (p. 44) "A phonological word in Palula may carry one, and only one, accent. Phonetically the accent is primarily realised as relatively higher pitch, accompanied to some extent by higher amplitude. ... The accent-bearing unit is the vocalic mora, which means that accent can be associated with a short vowel (as in (23)), or with the first mora of a long vowel (as in (24)), or with the second mora of a long vowel (as in (25))." (p. 72) "Even though some combinations of syllables and accents are more common than others and there are restrictions on accent placement (see below), the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined as lexical." (p. 73) "Accent falls either on the final or the penultimate syllable in a non-verbal lexical stem, as seen in (27) and (28); whereas in verbal stems, as in (29), the accent is always on the final syllable. In terms of vocalic moras, only one of the three last moras, of any lexical stem in Palula, may be the locus of the pitch accent." (p. 74)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word (bare stem or stem plus suffixes) carries exactly one accent, realised as higher pitch (with some extra amplitude) on a single vocalic mora: a short vowel, or the first (falling) or second (rising) mora of a long vowel. Its position is lexical within limits: on non-verbal stems it sits on the final or the penultimate syllable (one of the last three moras), on verbal stems always on the final syllable. Accent-bearing suffixes (plural -í, oblique -í, present -áan, infinitive -áai, etc.) remove the stem accent and take it themselves; accent-neutral suffixes normally leave the stem accent in place. Minimal pairs by accent position/mora exist (káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many?', čúur 'four' vs čuúr 'hot fire').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the grammar states a word 'may carry one, and only one, accent' (p. 72). The word 'stress' beyond the p. 44 summary is used only for a compound's 'primary stressed part' (p. 71) and for historical OIA accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Under certain conditions the stem accent shifts onto an accent-neutral suffix (§3.5.1, pp. 75ff., with segmental alternations, e.g. ṣiṣ~ṣiṣóom); a small class of 'accent-shifting T-verbs' (§9.3.7, p. 216); some suffix allomorphy (-áan/-éen/-áand). Morgenstierne 1941 (§9, p. 11) described stress impressionistically as falling on the first long syllable from the end, no further back than the antepenult, with no tone noticed; Liljegren's mora-accent analysis supersedes this.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem or stem+suffixes); the p. 44 statement refers to the lexical root, the p. 74 statement to lexical stems; suffix behaviour is stated separately. Postpositions 'tend to receive stress like other free morphemes' (p. 143). Description covers both main dialects, Ashret (A) and Biori (B), with A as primary.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog phal1254 Palula = Phalura/Phalūṛa (Morgenstierne 1941) = Dangarikwar/Ashreti; Liljegren 2016 covers both main dialects, Ashret (A, primary) and Biori (B), and states the accent facts for both. The related Sawi sketch (Bashir 2003, pp. 887-889) concerns a distinct language in Afghanistan, not this key.

new_statements.relation_note: already held by the project from the 2026-09-17 pass, re-read here. Differs in TYPE from the catalog's existing statement (Liljegren 2016: lexically defined mora pitch accent, not predictable): Morgenstierne describes a quantity-driven stress rule and explicitly denies any tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the rightmost long (heavy) syllable, limited to a three-syllable window at the right edge (never further left than the antepenult); in some words a long penult takes the stress even when the final is also long. No lexical or morphological tone noticed.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words stress a long penult even when the final syllable is long (examples given, scanned too noisy to transcribe reliably).
new_statements.identity_note: Liljegren 2016 describes both the Ashret and Biori dialects of Palula (Chitral); Liljegren & Haider 2009 is based on the Ashret variety (speaker Naseem Haider). new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has exactly one accent, realised mainly as higher pitch (with some extra amplitude); the accent-bearing unit is the mora, so a short vowel carries high/falling pitch and a long vowel carries either rising (second-mora) or falling (first-mora) pitch. Placement is lexical within a window: final or penultimate syllable of a non-verbal stem (one of the last three moras), always the final syllable of a verbal stem; minimal pairs exist (čúur 'four' vs čuúr 'hot fire', káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many', déedi vs deédi). Accent-bearing suffixes (mostly verbal: plural/oblique -í, present -áan, infinitive -áai, perfective -íl, causative -á, etc.) take the word accent off the stem; accent-neutral suffixes (person-number agreement, plural/oblique -a, -am, genitive -ii/-e) normally leave the stem accent, but stems with final-mora accent (all polysyllabic ones, some monosyllables unpredictably) shift the accent onto an accent-neutral suffix (putr / putr-á, kuṇaák / kuṇaak-á vs haát / háat-a), with accent-conditioned vowel alternations that differ between the Ashret and Biori dialects. Footnote 38 likens it to the Lithuanian / Ancient Greek mora accent 'free within limits'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the work states one and only one accent per phonological word. The only other remark is that in compounds of two aspirated words 'the primary stressed part of the compound keeps its aspiration' (p. 73), and that postpositions 'tend to receive stress' (p. 131 area, syntax), neither amounting to a secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal stems: accent always stem-final (no penult option). Accent shift to accent-neutral suffixes is predictable for polysyllabic final-mora-accented stems but lexically unpredictable for many monosyllabic stems (Table 15: dhut/dhút-a, haát/háat-a do not shift; putr/putr-á does). Accented suffix allomorphy: A. -am -> -óom when accented; B. -am -> -áam (closed syll.) / -úum (open), genitive -e -> -í when accented. Sec. 8.3.7 lists accent-shifting T-verbs. Acute mark omitted on monosyllables with short vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Palula of the Ashret valley by default ('if nothing is explicitly indicated it is the speech of Ashret that is intended', p. 43), with Biori-valley forms marked B. (Puri and Kalkatak treated as a sub-variety of Biori); the two dialects are stated to have identical segment and suprasegmental inventories, differing in accent-conditioned vowel alternations (Table 4, Tables 16-17).

This 2-way contrast is illustrated in Figure 1, showing f0 graphs of two Palula lexical items that are segmentally identical but contrast in terms of their respective fundamental frequencies. ... tone_statements.summary: Areal survey: Palula illustrates the 2-way 'Shina-type' tonal contrast (often called pitch accent), a word-level feature; f0 tracks of raát 'night' (rising) vs ráat 'blood' (falling). No inventory.

tone_statements.quote: Nouns with pitch accent on the last vocalic mora shift their accent from the stem to the suffix, a pattern observed also in Gilgiti ... Along with the lengthening of *a to aa, some of the vowels developed a first-mora (falling) accent and some of them a second-mora (rising) accent. ... A tentative comparison of the tonal patterns of Gawri and Klk carried out by Baart (pc) indicated that Klk may have developed the same type of tonal system seen in Gawri ... This stands in contrast to the simple pitch-accent system found in most other Shina varieties (including NP and SP).
tone_statements.summary: Comparative-historical paper; calls NP/SP Palula a 'simple pitch accent system', accent on 1st or 2nd mora of long vowels (acute-marked); no count; p.59 puts Pal in the Shina pitch accent area.

tone_statements.quote: Accented phonation is produced with front tensing, an upward pulling of the larynx that occurs along with normal back-tensed phonation. This process produces a raised F0. ... The position of accent on long vowels is distinctive. On long vowels with beginning accent, indicated by the accent mark placed before the vowel, front tensing occurs at the beginning of the vowel and then drops, producing a falling pitch throughout the vowel (see Fig. 2). On long vowels with ending accent, indicated by the accent mark placed after the vowel, front tensing occurs at the end of the vowel ... The result is a level, falling-rising, or rising pitch across the vowel, depending on the intensity of speech (see Fig. 3). Thus there is a contrast between, e.g., ending-accented râʹt 'night and day [24-hour period]' vs. beginning-accented rʹât 'blood'.
tone_statements.locator: web page 'The Sound System of aćharêtâʹ', section 'Phonation and Laryngeal Accent' (unpaginated HTML)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical pitch accent: raised-F0 accent on one vowel; on long vowels accent position contrastive (early = falling, late = rising/level), i.e. moraic accent; window = last two syllables of the word.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, between eras rather than within one: Morgenstierne 1941 (§9, p. 11) treats Palula as having quantity-sensitive stress (rightmost long syllable, not further back than the antepenult, with some long penults winning over long finals) and states he noticed no lexical or morphological tone, whereas Liljegren (& Haider 2009 p. 385; 2016 pp. 44, 73-74) analyses a lexically defined, culminative, mora-based pitch accent that is not predictable and yields minimal pairs. The two agree on the right-edge window (antepenult limit / last three moras) but differ on type and predictability; Liljegren's account, based on long-term fieldwork and instrumental phonetics, supersedes the 1941 notes. The only listed work (Liljegren 2008 thesis) could not be opened, so it neither confirms nor challenges this. No new conflict. The only divergent source remains Morgenstierne 1941 (held by the project from the earlier reading), who described dynamic stress on 'the first long syllable from the end, but not further back than the antepenultima' and noticed no relevant tone; Liljegren's window (last three moras, long vowels attracting first- or second-mora accent) largely covers the same surface facts but treats placement as lexical and the realisation as pitch, so the disagreement is one of analysis/type (weight-sensitive stress vs lexical pitch accent) between a 1941 field note and the modern full grammars, not between the modern sources.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik & Naseem Haider. 2009. Palula (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(3): 381-386. doi:10.1017/S0025100309990193
sources.quote: A phonological word in Palula may carry one, and only one, accent. Phonetically the accent is primarily realized as relatively higher pitch, accompanied to some extent by higher amplitude. [...] The accent-bearing unit is the mora. [...] Even though some combinations of syllables and accents are more common than others, and there are restrictions on accent placement, the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined lexically. In some cases, difference in accent placement is the only phonemic contrast between two lexical items: séeti 'thigh' vs. seetí 'having looked after'
sources.note: 'Pitch accent' section p. 385: 'A phonological word in Palula may carry one, and only one, accent', realised as higher pitch (and some amplitude); accent-bearing unit is the mora; 'the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined lexically'; minimal pairs séeti 'thigh' vs seetí 'having looked after', háar vs haár. Gives no positional rule beyond this (the grammar does).
sources.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik. 2008. Towards a grammatical description of Palula: An Indo-Aryan language of the Hindu Kush. PhD dissertation, Stockholm University.
sources.quote: p. 52: "Main stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical root. The stressed syllable receives pitch accent, phonetically realised as: a) high level or falling on a short vowel [ ́], represented in this work as á (in polysyllabic words, elsewhere no marking); b) rising on a long vowel [ ̌], represented aá; or c) falling on a long vowel [ ̂], represented as áa. Pitch accent is contrastive". p. 74: "A phonological word in Palula may carry one, and only one, accent. [...] The accent-bearing unit is the mora". p. 75: "the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined as lexical." p. 75: "Accent falls either in the final or the penultimate syllable in a non-verbal lexical stem [...] whereas in verbal stems [...] the accent is always on the final syllable."

sources.quote: Nouns with pitch accent on the last vocalic mora shift their accent from the stem to the suffix, a pattern observed also in Gilgiti ... Along with the lengthening of *a to aa, some of the vowels developed a first-mora (falling) accent and some of them a second-mora (rising) accent. ... A tentative comparison of the tonal patterns of Gawri and Klk carried out by Baart (pc) indicated that Klk may have developed the same type of tonal system seen in Gawri ... This stands in contrast to the simple pitch-accent system found in most other Shina varieties (including NP and SP).
sources.note: Comparative-historical paper; calls NP/SP Palula a 'simple pitch accent system', accent on 1st or 2nd mora of long vowels (acute-marked); no count; p.59 puts Pal in the Shina pitch accent area.

sources.quote: Accented phonation is produced with front tensing, an upward pulling of the larynx that occurs along with normal back-tensed phonation. This process produces a raised F0. ... The position of accent on long vowels is distinctive. On long vowels with beginning accent, indicated by the accent mark placed before the vowel, front tensing occurs at the beginning of the vowel and then drops, producing a falling pitch throughout the vowel (see Fig. 2). On long vowels with ending accent, indicated by the accent mark placed after the vowel, front tensing occurs at the end of the vowel ... The result is a level, falling-rising, or rising pitch across the vowel, depending on the intensity of speech (see Fig. 3). Thus there is a contrast between, e.g., ending-accented râʹt 'night and day [24-hour period]' vs. beginning-accented rʹât 'blood'.

tone.translation: The local character of this process was shown by me on the material of the Dardic language Shina, which has preserved the Old Indic free (mobile) accent. In this language, in such forms ... this shift did not take place: all such stems in it have root accent. The same situation holds in the Dardic languages Dameli, Phalura and Maiyan.
